\title{A Temporal FRBR/FRBRoo-Based Model for \\ Component-Level Versioning of Legal Norms}

\author[1]{Hudson de Martim}
\affil[1]{Federal Senate of Brazil \\ \texttt{hudsonm@senado.leg.br}}
\date{} % No date printed

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Effectively representing legal norms for automated processing is a critical challenge, particularly in tracking the diachronic evolution of their hierarchical components (e.g., articles, paragraphs). While foundational frameworks like FRBR/FRBRoo and standards like Akoma Ntoso model legal documents at a macro level, they lack native mechanisms for granular, component-level versioning. This limitation hinders the deterministic point-in-time reconstruction of legal texts, a fundamental capability for reliable Legal Tech and AI applications.
This paper proposes a structured, temporal model that extends the FRBRoo framework to address this gap. It introduces specialized subclasses of Expression—Temporal Version (TV) and Language Version (LV)—to represent the state of a legal norm and its linguistic variations at specific points in time. The model applies this same paradigm hierarchically, introducing Component Work (CW), Component Temporal Version (CTV), and Component Language Version (CLV) to track the lifecycle of individual articles, paragraphs, and clauses.
Using the Brazilian Federal Constitution as a case study, the paper demonstrates how each amendment creates new Component Temporal Versions for affected provisions, while unaffected components retain their existing versions. This fine-grained, time-aware architecture enables the precise, deterministic retrieval and reconstruction of any part of a legal text as it existed on a specific date. The model provides a robust foundation for developing advanced legal information systems, knowledge graphs, and AI tools capable of accurate historical analysis and impact assessment, overcoming the limitations of current generative models.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} FRBRoo; Temporal Modeling; Legal Knowledge Graph; Legal Text Evolution; Component-Level Versioning; Akoma Ntoso; LexML.

\section{Introduction}
The increasing demand for transparency, efficiency in legal research, and the proliferation of Legal Tech and Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications underscore the critical need for machine-readable representations of legal norms \cite{kucuk2025computational}. Effectively representing these norms for automated processing, however, requires a nuanced approach that captures not only the entirety of a legal instrument but also its constituent parts and, crucially, its dynamic state over time \cite{chen2023temporal} \cite{cai2024survey}.

While foundational conceptual frameworks—such as the Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records (FRBR/FRBRoo) and the XML schema standard Akoma Ntoso—provide robust approaches for representing legal documents and their macro-level evolution \cite{lima2008ontology}, they typically focus on entire instruments (\emph{Works}/\emph{Expressions}/\emph{Manifestations}) rather than on sub-documentary elements. Although the OASIS LegalDocML initiative and related European modeling efforts (e.g., OntoLegis) have shown how to encode legislative texts in XML, these initiatives do not fully address the need to track temporally discrete, component-level changes (titles, articles, paragraphs) with explicit versioning metadata.

This challenge is particularly acute when considering the capabilities of current Generative AI. For instance, Brazil’s 1988 Federal Constitution has been amended over one hundred times since its enactment. Each amendment may insert, delete, or modify specific articles and paragraphs.Today's large language models (LLMs) and other generative AI tools operate on a 
probabilistic basis, which, despite their substantial capabilities, makes them inherently 
unsuitable for tasks requiring absolute precision. They lack deterministic mechanisms to 
retrieve or reconstruct the exact text of the Constitution as it stood on a particular past date 
(e.g., January 10, 2005), frequently leading to inadvertent omissions or discrepancies. This 
limitation highlights a critical gap, as the high-stakes nature of the legal field demands 
verifiable accuracy and deterministic reliability, where correctness is not a probability but a requirement.

Against this backdrop, the present paper proposes and details a specialized adaptation of the FRBRoo conceptual model—augmented by Akoma Ntoso-inspired metadata conventions—to deliver a fully structured, semantically-rich representation of Brazilian legal norms and their diachronic evolution. We demonstrate how FRBRoo’s core concepts (\emph{Work}, \emph{Expression}, \emph{Manifestation}) can be extended into a multi-tier hierarchy that captures not only the normative instrument as a whole but also its internal elements (titles, chapters, articles, paragraphs) and each of those elements’ variants across time and language. Crucially, this paper advances the FRBRoo model by introducing two complementary refinements: \emph{Temporal Version}, which is a subclass of \emph{Expression} specifically designed to capture the exact textual state of a norm (or its components) on a given date, and \emph{Language Version}, which encapsulates the linguistic variants of a given expression in different official languages.

By instantiating a \emph{Temporal Version} for each amendment event—and linking that version deterministically to the relevant \emph{Work} and \emph{Manifestation}—we achieve a precise, date-specific representation of the legal norm (and its components). Similarly, \emph{Language Version} objects allow the system to maintain parallel translations of each \emph{Temporal Version}. This fine-grained, time-aware architecture forms the basis for building deterministic pipelines capable of reconstructing compiled (unofficial consolidated) texts as they existed at any point in history, thus overcoming present limitations of generative AI models. By doing so, our model establishes the verifiable factual ground truth required for advanced computational legal reasoning systems to operate reliably.

This paper is structured as follows. Section \ref{fundamental_concepts} reviews foundational concepts from the FRBRoo model and examines related legal information frameworks, including LexML Brazil and Akoma Ntoso, highlighting their treatment of norm identity, structure, and temporality. Section \ref{legal_norm_representation} introduces our core proposal: a structured, temporally-aware model for representing legal norms grounded in the Work–Expression–Manifestation (WEM) framework. Section \ref{legal_norm_component_representation} details how this model is extended to represent the internal hierarchical components of norms (e.g., articles, paragraphs, clauses), introducing the notions of Component Work (CW), Component Temporal Version (CTV), and Component Language Version (CLV) and discusses the temporal evolution and multilingual expression of components, using the caput of Article 6 of the Brazilian Federal Constitution as a detailed example. Section \ref{sec:conclusion_future_work} concludes the paper and outlines future research directions, including formal ontology development, knowledge graph implementation, and integration with AI and NLP applications.

\section{Fundamental Concepts}
\label{fundamental_concepts}
To ground our proposal in established theory, this section reviews how existing frameworks—namely LexML Brazil and Akoma Ntoso—leverage the FRBRoo concepts of \emph{Work}, \emph{Expression}.

\subsection{FRBRoo Overview}
The Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records (FRBRoo) model, originally developed by the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA) for bibliographic cataloging \cite{bekiari2008frbroo}, provides a conceptual framework for understanding information resources. FRBRoo, an object-oriented version harmonized with the CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model (CIDOC CRM), extends this framework into a formal ontology, enhancing its applicability across diverse domains, including the legal field.

The core of the FRBRoo model lies in its clear distinction between the abstract intellectual or artistic content and its various physical and representational forms. It defines three main entities:
\begin{itemize}
    \item a \emph{Work} (FRBRoo F1), representing a distinct abstract intellectual creation. In the legal domain, this corresponds to the normative intent or conceptual scope of a law, independent of any particular textual instantiation.
    \item an \emph{Expression} (FRBRoo F2), representing a specific realization of a Work. This includes, for example, the text of a statute in a given language or version. Through CIDOC CRM’s \emph{E52 Time-Span}, FRBRoo can record validity periods for each Expression, enabling temporal annotations.
    \item a \emph{Manifestation} (FRBRoo F3 or F4), representing the physical or digital carrier of an Expression. In practice, this may be an official gazette publication, or any other distribution format.
\end{itemize}
Additionally, an \emph{Item} (FRBRoo F5) represents a single exemplar of a Manifestation, such as a specific printed copy.

This tripartite distinction is particularly powerful in the legal domain. The abstract normative intent of a legal norm (\emph{Work}) is distinct from its specific authoritative textual formulation in a given language (\emph{Expression}), and is again distinct from its various published formats (\emph{Manifestation}). By leveraging CIDOC CRM’s temporal constructs, each \emph{Expression} can be associated with explicit start and end dates, thus capturing its valid time-span. Such temporal annotation is essential for tracking amendments, translations, and the evolution of legal texts over time.

The following subsections discuss how established legal information initiatives, Akoma Ntoso and  LexML Brazil, have adopted and operationalized these FRBRoo concepts, including their strategies (or gaps) in temporal modeling.

\subsection{Akoma Ntoso Approach}
Akoma Ntoso (AKN) \cite{palmirani2011akoma} is an XML vocabulary specifically designed for representing parliamentary, legislative, judicial, and soft law documents in a machine-readable format. Its conceptual design is aligned with FRBRoo, providing a structured framework for legal documents at different levels of abstraction:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Work}: In AKN, the abstract legal content (the \emph{Work}) is identified through unique identifiers (e.g., the \texttt{<FRBRWork>} element). This allows consistent references to the underlying legal concept, independently of text variants or publication forms.

    \item \textbf{Expression}: AKN models the specific authoritative text (the \emph{Expression}) within elements such as \texttt{<FRBRExpression>}. It separates text content from metadata, enabling detailed semantic annotations (e.g., through \texttt{<paragraph>}, \texttt{<article>}, and semantic tag sets). Multilingual support is provided via separate \texttt{<FRBRExpression>} entries for each language version.

    \item \textbf{Manifestation}: The physical or digital carrier of an Expression (the \emph{Manifestation}) is represented by elements like \texttt{<FRBRManifestation>}, which capture details such as format (XML, HTML, PDF) and publication metadata (e.g., \texttt{<publicationDate>}, \texttt{<version>}).
\end{itemize}

Although AKN provides mechanisms to record publication dates and version identifiers at the document level, it does not natively support fine-grained temporal annotations for individual components (such as articles or paragraphs). In practice, one can include timestamps via custom attributes or extended metadata, but AKN’s core schema lacks built-in constructs to track, for example, when a specific article was amended or replaced. Consequently, while AKN excels at structural and semantic tagging, it requires additional conventions or extensions to capture the component-level, time-specific versions that our proposal will formalize.  

This reveals a fundamental distinction in modeling approaches. While Akoma Ntoso, for example, 
provides mechanisms to record temporal metadata, it largely leaves the interpretation and 
application of complex temporal logic---especially at a granular, component level---to external 
processes or systems.

In contrast, our proposed model explicitly reifies these temporal states as distinct ontological 
entities (namely, as subclasses of \texttt{F22 SelfContainedExpression}). This design choice 
makes the temporal evolution and relationships of legal texts and their components explicit 
\emph{within the ontology itself}, rather than depending on the implicit interpretation of 
metadata attributes. This distinction is critical for AI applications. Implicit temporal data 
requires complex, often heuristic-based reasoning engines to infer the correct textual 
state at a given point in time. By modeling each temporal state as an explicit entity, 
however, our approach drastically simplifies deterministic reconstruction, querying, and reasoning. 
The strength of our proposal thus lies in its commitment to making these implicit temporal 
dynamics explicit and formally structured.

\subsection{LexML Brazil Approach}
The LexML Brazil project\footnote{LexML Brazil, Legislative Integration Project. Available at: \url{https://projeto.lexml.gov.br}. Accessed on: 08 Jun 2025.} explicitly adopts the FRBRoo as its foundational reference for legislative and legal information. FRBRoo enables the representation of both the creation process of a work—captured as a \emph{Work} and its \emph{Expression} embodied in an original (Singleton \emph{Manifestation})—and the subsequent reproduction process that yields multiple copies (\emph{Items}) of that original.

According to the LexML Reference Model \cite{lexml2023modelo}, legislative and legal information can be perceived at three levels of abstraction:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Physical or Digital Object} (\emph{Manifestation}): for example, the original document signed by the President of the Republic (the \emph{autograph} or \texttt{<F4 Manifestation>}) or the PDF published by the Official Gazette (\texttt{<F3 Manifestation Product Type>}).
    \item \textbf{Linguistic Object} (\emph{Expression}): the textual content conveyed by these media (e.g., \texttt{<F2 Expression>} in a particular language).
    \item \textbf{Semantic Object} (\emph{Work}): the normative content or legal intent conveyed in the text (e.g., \texttt{<F1 Work>} representing the abstract legal norm).
\end{itemize}

LexML’s core tenet is that a legal norm (\emph{Work}) is created at the moment of its signature by the competent authority, and its publication is the mechanism through which it enters into force. To support this lifecycle, LexML uses the following temporal metadata:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \texttt{<dataRepresentativa>} (representative date): the date of signature, which identifies an instance of an \texttt{<F15 ComplexWork>} corresponding to the new norm.
    \item \texttt{<dataVersao>} (effective date): the date when a specific version of the norm becomes valid.
    \item \texttt{<dataVisao>} (versioning event date): the date of an event that generates a new version or variant of the norm (e.g., rectification, repeal, or declaration of unconstitutionality).
\end{itemize}

These temporal attributes allow LexML to identify and distinguish different document-level versions and variants over time. However, LexML does not natively provide explicit temporal annotations for individual components (such as an article or paragraph). While it is possible to include custom attributes or extended metadata within the XML schema, the core model applies temporal markers at the norm level rather than at finer granularity. Consequently, LexML ensures that the abstract norm, its authoritative text, and its public embodiments remain distinct yet interconnected, but it leaves a gap in tracking component-level changes—precisely the gap our proposed model aims to fill.

It is worth noting that the LexML URN standard, with its \texttt{norm@version\textasciitilde language!part} 
syntax, provides an advanced and powerful \textbf{identification scheme} for temporal components. 
This syntax correctly acknowledges the need to uniquely address a specific part of a norm as it existed 
on a given date. However, an identification scheme is not a representation model in itself. The URN acts 
as a pointer to a resource but does not formally define the relationships between resources. For instance, 
it does not explicitly model that \texttt{!art6\_cpt@2000-02-14} supersedes a previous version or that 
both are temporal expressions of the same abstract \emph{Component Work}. Our proposed FRBRoo-based model 
provides precisely this missing semantic layer: the formal, explicit representation of entities and their 
diachronic relationships, thereby supplying the necessary ontological foundation to fully leverage such a 
powerful naming convention in a deterministic system.

It is important to situate our contribution within the broader academic landscape of temporal 
versioning for legal knowledge. Research into temporal ontology versioning \cite{grandi2009valid}  \cite{zekri2016tauowl} addresses the critical challenge of managing the evolution of 
the ontology itself---that is, the changes in abstract concepts, properties, and logical rules 
over time. Our model addresses a distinct yet complementary problem. We focus specifically on versioning  the \textbf{textual realization} of legal norms (the FRBRoo \texttt{F22 Expression}) and their hierarchical components. We are 
providing the stable, versioned \emph{textual ground truth} that is a necessary prerequisite 
for any subsequent semantic modeling or logical reasoning. Clarifying this focus highlights our 
unique contribution and avoids perceived redundancy with works centered on conceptual-level 
versioning.

\section{FRBRoo-Based Representation of Legal Norms}
\label{legal_norm_representation}
The FRBRoo model, originally developed for library cataloging, has proven highly adaptable for describing complex information resources across various domains, including legal information. In this section, we detail how FRBRoo’s core entities—\emph{Work}, \emph{Expression}, and \emph{Manifestation}—map to the lifecycle of a legal norm, preparing the ground for our subsequent introduction of temporal and language refinements.

When applied to legal norms, this tripartite distinction is instantiated as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Work.} The legal norm represents the abstract intellectual content or fundamental legal idea established through the legislative process. It is the “what” of the legal norm, independent of any textual formulation or medium. In practice, the \emph{Work} is formalized at the moment of its signature (i.e., its official promulgation) by the competent authority, marking the conclusion of the legislative process.\footnote{It is important to clarify that this model represents the \emph{product} of the legislative process---the final, enacted norm and its subsequent temporal states---rather than modeling the legislative \emph{procedure} itself (e.g., bill drafting, debates, or voting)}. This aligns with the LexML Brazil project’s approach, which identifies the \emph{Work} using a specific subclass of \texttt{<F1 Work>}---namely, \texttt{<F15 ComplexWork>}\footnote{In FRBRoo, an \texttt{F15 ComplexWork} represents a bibliographic Work that is composed of multiple intellectual Works, such as compilations or consolidated collections of laws.}---to capture its aggregate nature. The identification is made via the \texttt{<dataRepresentativa>} element (date of signature).

    \item \textbf{Expression.} An \emph{Expression} is the specific linguistic and intellectual realization of a \emph{Work}. For a legal norm, this corresponds to the authoritative textual formulation as drafted and signed by the competent authority at the culmination of the legislative process. LexML models the original signed document as an \texttt{<F4 ManifestationSingleton>}\footnote{In FRBRoo, an \texttt{F4 ManifestationSingleton} represents a unique physical object that embodies a single Expression, such as an original manuscript or signed decree.} containing an \texttt{<F22 SelfContainedExpression>}\footnote{In FRBRoo, an \texttt{F22 SelfContainedExpression} represents a complete, distinct realization of a Work’s content.}, which holds the normative text. Distinct linguistic versions (for example, an English translation of a Portuguese statute) are modeled as separate \emph{Expressions} of the same \emph{Work}.

    \item \textbf{Manifestation.} A \emph{Manifestation} is the physical or digital carrier of an \emph{Expression}. In the legal domain, this refers primarily to the official publication venue—commonly the Official Gazette—where the norm is made publicly accessible and thereby acquires legal force. Different file formats or publication media (for example, an HTML page versus a PDF rendition of the same gazette issue) are considered distinct \emph{Manifestations}. An \emph{Item} (modeled as \texttt{<F5 Item>} in FRBRoo) is a single exemplar of a \emph{Manifestation}, such as one printed copy of the Official Gazette or one downloaded PDF file.
\end{itemize}

By clearly distinguishing these three levels, we can model a legal norm’s lifecycle from its abstract conception (\emph{Work}) through its authoritative text (\emph{Expression}) to its public dissemination (\emph{Manifestation}), while also accounting for multiple language renditions and publication formats. In Section~\ref{legal_norm_component_representation}, we will extend this base model by introducing \emph{Temporal Version} and \emph{Language Version} refinements, which enable fine-grained tracking of component-level changes (e.g., individual articles or paragraphs) over time and across languages.

\subsection{Practical Mapping of Work, Expression, and Manifestation}
\label{sec:work_expression_manifestation_practice}
The FRBRoo model defines an \emph{Expression} as a specific intellectual realization of a \emph{Work}. In particular, FRBRoo’s \texttt{<F22 SelfContainedExpression>} class represents a complete, standalone textual realization of a Work. Building on this, we introduce two specialized subclasses of \texttt{<F22 SelfContained Expression>}, which is a subclass of \texttt{<F2 Expression>}:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Temporal Version (TV).} A subclass of \texttt{<F22 SelfContainedExpression>} that captures the exact textual state of a legal norm on a specific date or event. In other words, each \emph{TV} is a dated \emph{Expression} of the \emph{Work}. Formally:
    \[
      \texttt{TemporalVersion} \;\sqsubseteq\; \texttt{F22 SelfContainedExpression}
    \]
    where \texttt{TemporalVersion} includes mandatory properties such as \texttt{validFromDate} and (optionally) \texttt{validToDate} to record its precise time span.

    \item \textbf{Language Version (LV).} A subclass of \texttt{F22 SelfContainedExpression} that represents a monolingual textual realization derived from a given \emph{Temporal Version}. Each \emph{LV} is therefore a language-specific \emph{Expression} of the same \emph{Work}. Formally:
    \[
      \texttt{LanguageVersion} \;\sqsubseteq\; \texttt{F22 SelfContainedExpression}
    \]
    and is linked to exactly one \emph{Temporal Version} via a property such as \texttt{derivesFromTemporal Version}.
\end{itemize}

In FRBRoo notation:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Each \texttt{TemporalVersion} is an instance of \texttt{<F22 SelfContainedExpression>} enriched with temporal properties (e.g., \texttt{E52 Time-Span} from CIDOC CRM).
    \item Each \texttt{LanguageVersion} is an instance of \texttt{<F22 SelfContainedExpression>} extended by a \texttt{language} attribute (ISO 639-1 code) and a \texttt{derivesFromTemporalVersion} relationship.
\end{itemize}

Figure~\ref{fig:norm_versions_publications} illustrates how a single \emph{Work} (the abstract norm) may have multiple \emph{Temporal Versions} (each a dated \texttt{<F22 SelfContainedExpression>}), and how each \emph{Temporal Version} may have one or more \emph{Language Versions} (also \texttt{F22} instances with a specific \texttt{language}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.7\textwidth]{Figure4.jpg}
    \caption{Relationship among Norm (\emph{Work}), \texttt{TemporalVersion} (\emph{F22 SelfContainedExpression}), \texttt{LanguageVersion} (\emph{F22 SelfContainedExpression}), and \emph{Manifestation}.}
    \label{fig:norm_versions_publications}
\end{figure}

By defining \emph{Temporal Version} and \emph{Language Version} as explicit subclasses of \texttt{<F22 SelfContained Expression>}, we maintain strict alignment with FRBRoo while clarifying that each “version” is, in fact, a specialized kind of \emph{Expression}. 

In jurisdictions with multiple official languages—such as Canada or the European Union—a legal norm’s \emph{Temporal Version} is inherently multilingual, comprising one distinct \emph{Language Version} for each official language.

In contrast, in monolingual jurisdictions (including Brazil), each \emph{Temporal Version} is effectively monolingual, so the single \emph{Language Version} coincides with the \emph{Temporal Version} (see Figure~\ref{fig:monolingual_countries}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{Figure5.jpg}
    \caption{Monolingual case (Portuguese): Temporal Versions (\emph{TV}) and Language Versions (\emph{LV}) coincide.}
    \label{fig:monolingual_countries}
\end{figure}

The \textbf{Signed Document} of the original version—whether a physical paper with a handwritten signature or a digitally signed authoritative file—depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:monolingual_countries} is the first and most authoritative \emph{Manifestation} of that version. In FRBRoo terms, this is an \texttt{<F4 ManifestationSingleton>} if it is a unique physical object.

The \textbf{Official Publication} of the original version (e.g., in the Official Gazette) is a subsequent \emph{Manifestation}, intended for public dissemination and to confer broader legal effect or notice. It reproduces the content of the original \emph{Expression}, typically as an \texttt{<F3 ManifestationProductType>} when mass‐produced (e.g., multiple copies of the gazette issue).

By distinguishing \emph{Temporal Versions} (as \emph{Expressions}) and their derived \emph{Language Versions}, and by linking each \emph{LV} to its respective \emph{Manifestation}, we establish a clear, deterministic mapping that supports precise point‐in‐time retrieval and accurate consolidation of legal texts.  

\subsubsection{Practical Brazilian Example}
\label{sec:practical_brazilian_example}

To illustrate these concepts, consider the FRBR \emph{Work} corresponding to the Brazilian Federal Constitution of 1988. Using the LexML URN format\footnote{LexML URN syntax follows the standard proposed by the Brazilian LexML project. Available at: \url{https://projeto.lexml.gov.br}. Accessed on: 15 Mar 2025.}, the \emph{Work} is identified as:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988}
\end{itemize}

Its original \emph{Temporal Version}—the textual formulation of the norm on the date of signature—is identified by appending \texttt{@YYYY-MM-DD}:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05} (\texttt{@1988-10-05} indicates the version date)
\end{itemize}

Because this initial \emph{Temporal Version} is monolingual (Portuguese, \texttt{pt}), its \emph{Language Version} has the same text but is assigned a distinct URN to reflect its conceptual role:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;pt} (\texttt{\textasciitilde texto;pt} indicates Portuguese content)
\end{itemize}

This \emph{Portuguese Language Version} can be delivered via multiple \emph{Manifestations}. For example:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;pt$text-html} (\texttt{\$text-html} represents html support)
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;pt$text-pdf} (\texttt{\$text-pdf} represents pdf support)
\end{itemize}

If this original \emph{Portuguese Language Version} is later translated into English (\texttt{en}), a new \emph{Language Version} is created with its own URN:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;en} (\texttt{\textasciitilde texto;en} indicates English content)
\end{itemize}

That English \emph{Language Version} will have its own \emph{Manifestations}, such as:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;en$text-html} (\texttt{\$text-html} represents html support)
\end{itemize}

In summary, for the 1988 Constitution:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The \emph{Work} is identified by the base URN without a date suffix.
    \item Each \emph{Temporal Version} adds “\texttt{@YYYY-MM-DD}” to capture the text’s state on that date.
    \item Each \emph{Language Version} adds “\texttt{\textasciitilde texto;LL}” (where \texttt{LL} is the language code).
    \item Each \emph{Manifestation} appends “\texttt{\$text-<format>}” to denote the delivery format.
\end{enumerate}

This approach ensures that every distinct stage—abstract \emph{Work}, dated \emph{Temporal Version}, language‐specific \emph{Language Version}, and each \emph{Manifestation}—receives a unique URN, enabling precise, deterministic retrieval and consolidation of the legal text at any given point in time.

\subsection{Legal Norm Compilation}
\label{sec:legal_norm_compilation}

In Brazil, a \emph{Compilation} (``Compilação'' in Portuguese) is the process by which, starting from a specified \emph{Temporal Version} (TV\textsubscript{0}) of a legal norm—such as the original text—all modifications introduced by subsequent amending acts up to a target date \(D\) are incorporated, thereby producing an (unofficial) consolidated text, denoted as TV\textsubscript{n} at date \(D\).

As defined previously, each \emph{Temporal Version} (TV) captures the precise textual state of a norm at a particular point in time. When a new legislative act amends an existing norm, it always applies to the \emph{most recent Temporal Version} of that norm, yielding a new, subsequent TV. For example, consider the Brazilian Federal Constitution of 1988:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1988-10-05:} TV\textsubscript{0}, the inaugural \emph{Temporal Version} corresponding to the original promulgation.
    \item \textbf{1992-03-31:} TV\textsubscript{1}, resulting from \emph{Constitutional Amendment No.~1 of 1992-03-31}, which modified TV\textsubscript{0}.
    \item \textbf{1993-03-17:} TV\textsubscript{2}, created when \emph{Constitutional Amendment No.~3 of 1993-03-17} amended TV\textsubscript{1}.
    \item \textbf{1993-09-14:} TV\textsubscript{3}, due to \emph{Constitutional Amendment No.~4 of 1993-09-14} amending TV\textsubscript{2}.
\end{itemize}
Note that \emph{Constitutional Amendment No.~2 of 1992-08-25} did not alter the text of the Constitution and therefore did not generate a new Temporal Version of the primary norm.

To generate a compiled \emph{Temporal Version} TV\textsubscript{n} of a norm at a given date \(D\), where \(n > 0\), the compilation process requires:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The immediately preceding compiled \emph{Temporal Version}, TV\textsubscript{n-1}, of the same norm.
    \item The original \emph{Temporal Versions} (TV\textsubscript{0}) of any amending norms that took effect on \(D\) and whose modifications target TV\textsubscript{n-1}.
\end{enumerate}

Those amending acts (each TV\textsubscript{0} of an amendment) are applied to TV\textsubscript{n-1} to produce TV\textsubscript{n}, which represents the consolidated (editorial) text of the norm on date \(D\). In FRBRoo terms, TV\textsubscript{n} would be modeled as a new instance of \texttt{TemporalVersion} with a \texttt{consolidates} property listing TV\textsubscript{n-1} and the relevant TV\textsubscript{0} instances of the amending acts as its sources.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{Figure3.jpg}
    \caption{Relationships among Temporal Versions reflecting the compilation process.}
    \label{fig:relationships_versions}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:relationships_versions} illustrates this process:  TV\textsubscript{n} is linked to TV\textsubscript{n-1} and to all TV\textsubscript{0} of amending acts via the \texttt{consolidates} property, enabling deterministic reconstruction of the compiled (unofficial consolidated) text on any target date.

By formalizing \emph{Compilation} in this way, we ensure that every compiled (unofficial consolidated) \emph{Temporal Version} can be precisely traced back to its immediate predecessor and all relevant amending acts, thereby supporting accurate, point-in-time retrieval and editorial consolidation of legal norms.

\section{Legal Norm’s Components Representation}
\label{legal_norm_component_representation}
Legal norms are not monolithic entities; they possess an internal hierarchical structure. This structure is composed of various \emph{Components}, which are identifiable, addressable subdivisions of the legal text below the level of the norm as a whole. These components serve to organize the normative content and often convey distinct legal propositions. Common examples include titles, chapters, sections, articles, “caput,” paragraphs, items, and clauses (or subitems). Just as the overarching legal norm evolves and can be expressed in multiple languages, so too can its individual components.

The challenge, therefore, is to represent not only the norm in its entirety but also each of its constituent parts in a way that captures their individual semantic content, their linguistic variations, and their temporal evolution. This granular approach is essential for precise legal analysis, accurate information retrieval, and enabling sophisticated AI applications that can reason about specific parts of a law over time.

\subsection{Applying the FRBRoo Model to Components}
\label{sec:applying_frbr_to_components}

Mirroring the representation of the legal norm as a whole (Section~\ref{legal_norm_representation}), each individual Component can also be conceptualized through the FRBRoo lens of \emph{Work}, \emph{Expression}, and \emph{Manifestation}. This ensures a uniform modeling paradigm across all levels of a legal text’s hierarchy.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Component Work (CW).} Represents the abstract normative content of a specific component (e.g., the legal rule conveyed by an article’s caput, or the scope defined by a chapter’s title). It is the “what” of that textual subdivision, independent of wording or language. Formally, each CW corresponds to a FRBRoo \texttt{<F1 Work>} at the component level and persists even when its Expression changes due to amendments.

    \item \textbf{Component Expression.} A specific realization of a \emph{Component Work}. We introduce two specialized subclasses:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Component Temporal Version (CTV).} A subclass of FRBRoo \texttt{<F22 SelfContained Expression>} that captures the exact textual state of a Component Work at a given point in time. The first CTV corresponds to the component’s original text as enacted. Each amendment affecting that component yields a new CTV, each annotated with a \texttt{validFromDate} (and optionally \texttt{validToDate}), recording its effective period.

        \item \textbf{Component Language Version (CLV).} A subclass of FRBRoo \texttt{<F22 SelfContained Expression>} that represents a monolingual realization of a specific CTV. Each CLV is linked to exactly one CTV (via a property such as \texttt{derivesFromComponentTemporalVersion}) and carries a \texttt{language} attribute (ISO 639-1 code). For example, the original Portuguese text of CTV\textsubscript{0} is a CLV; if an English translation is later created, that is a separate CLV of the same CTV.
    \end{itemize}

    \item \textbf{Component Manifestation (CM).} A physical or digital embodiment of a CLV. Although uncommon in practice (since components usually appear embedded in a larger document), CM can be modeled as instances of FRBRoo \texttt{<F3 ManifestationProductType>} (for mass-distributed formats) or \texttt{<F4 ManifestationSingleton>} (for unique artifacts). For example, a standalone PDF file containing only the text of Title I would be a CM of the corresponding CLV.
\end{itemize}

By treating each component as a mini-\emph{Work} with its own temporal and language Expressions (CTV and CLV), and optional Manifestations, we achieve full granularity. Each CW has a lifecycle: multiple CTVs (each dated), each spawning one or more CLVs (each language-specific), which may in turn be linked to individual CMs if needed. This detailed structure enables precise, component-level tracking of amendments, multilingual versions, and publication formats.

\subsection{Temporal Evolution and Multilingualism of Components}
\label{sec:temporal_evolution_multilingualism}

The critical insight here is that legal amendments often target specific components within a norm, rather than the entire document. When an amending norm modifies, adds, or revokes a component (e.g., changes the wording of a paragraph, adds a new item to an article, or repeals an entire section), it effectively creates a new \emph{Component Temporal Version} (CTV) for that specific component. The \emph{Component Work} associated with that structural position persists (e.g., the concept of “Article X” remains), but its textual realization changes. Components not affected by the amendment retain their existing CTVs.

This component-level versioning is essential. It allows us to precisely track what changed, when it changed, and what the exact text of any part of a norm was on any given date. Similarly, if a component’s text, as defined by a specific CTV, is translated into another language, this creates a new \emph{Component Language Version} (CLV) linked to that CTV.

Notably, the \texttt{consolidates} property, introduced in Section \ref{sec:legal_norm_compilation} to describe the compilation of a norm as a whole, applies with the same logic at this granular level. When an amendment modifies a specific component, the newly created Component Temporal Version (CTV) can be formally modeled as compiling (consolidating) two sources: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Its immediate predecessor CTV (the text before the change).
    \item The CTV 0 (original) of the specific modifying component from the amending legal norm's (the text that dictates the change).
\end{enumerate}
This ensures a consistent, recursive modeling pattern across all hierarchical levels of the legal text, 
reinforcing the model's structural robustness and analytical power for tracing changes with precision.

\subsubsection{Practical Example: Caput of Article 6 of the Brazilian Federal Constitution of 1988}
\label{sec:practical_example_component}

Consider the caput (main provision) of Article 6 of the Brazilian Federal Constitution of 1988, which enumerates social rights. The abstract concept and normative intent (the \textbf{Component Work}, CW) of defining fundamental social rights are identified using the LexML URN format\footnote{LexML URN syntax follows the standard proposed by the Brazilian LexML project. Available at: \url{https://projeto.lexml.gov.br}. Accessed on: 15 Mar 2025.} as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988!art6_cpt}
\end{itemize}

Its original \textbf{Component Temporal Version (CTV)}—the textual formulation of the caput on the date of signature—is identified by appending \texttt{@YYYY-MM-DD!<component\_id>}:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05!art6_cpt} (\texttt{@1988-10-05} indicates the version date)
\end{itemize}

Because this initial CTV is monolingual (Portuguese, \texttt{pt}), its \textbf{Component Language Version (CLV)} has the same text but is assigned a distinct URN to reflect its conceptual role:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;pt!art6_cpt} (\texttt{\textasciitilde texto;pt} indicates Portuguese content)
\end{itemize}

If this original Portuguese CLV is later translated into English (\texttt{en}), a new CLV is created with its own URN:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@1988-10-05~texto;en!art6_cpt} (\texttt{\textasciitilde texto;en} indicates English content)
\end{itemize}

The text of the original CTV (and CLV) of the caput of Article 6 is:
\begin{quote}\small
“São direitos sociais a educação, a saúde, o trabalho, o lazer, a segurança, a previdência social, a proteção à maternidade e à infância, a assistência aos desamparados, na forma desta Constituição.”\\
(“\textit{Social rights include education, health, work, leisure, security, social security, protection of motherhood and childhood, and assistance to the destitute, as prescribed by this Constitution.}”)
\end{quote}

Over time, this caput has been amended by several Constitutional Amendments (Emendas Constitucionais – EC), each creating a new CTV (and CLV) for this component. For example, Constitutional Amendment No.~26/2000 (EC 26/2000) of 2000-02-14 added “housing” (“moradia”) into the caput text. Consequently, a new CTV (and CLV) was created:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{CTV}:\newline
      \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@2000-02-14!art6_cpt}
    \item \textbf{CLV}:\newline
      \url{https://normas.leg.br/?urn=urn:lex:br:federal:constituicao:1988-10-05;1988@2000-02-14~texto;pt!art6_cpt}
\end{itemize}

In this example, the \emph{Component Work} (the concept of Article 6 caput defining social rights) remains unchanged, but a new \emph{Component Temporal Version} (CTV) reflects the textual state after the amendment. Subsequent translations or other format-specific \emph{Component Manifestations} can then be created for each new CLV.

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusion_future_work}
This paper has proposed and detailed a structured, temporal model for representing legal norms and their hierarchical components, grounded in the FRBRoo concepts of \emph{Work}, \emph{Expression}, and \emph{Manifestation}. By extending these principles from the entire norm down to its individual articles, paragraphs, and other subdivisions—introducing the notions of \emph{Temporal Versions} (TV/CTV) and \emph{Language Versions} (LV/CLV) at both levels—our proposal offers several key advantages:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Precision in Temporal Tracking:} Enables the exact history of each textual part of a norm to be recorded and retrieved, facilitating precise determination of its wording on any given date.
    \item \textbf{Targeted Impact Analysis:} Facilitates accurate mapping of an amendment’s impact to the specific components it affects, producing new \emph{Component Temporal Versions} (CTVs) only for those components.
    \item \textbf{Enhanced Information Retrieval:} Supports queries targeted at individual components and their historical versions, improving the accuracy and relevance of search results within complex legal corpora.
    \item \textbf{Deterministic Reconstruction:} In direct contrast to the probabilistic and 
    approximative nature of generative AI, our model enables the unambiguous, bit-by-bit 
    reconstruction of legal texts for any point in time. This focus on determinism provides 
    the reliability and verifiability that are primordial for high-stakes legal applications, 
    establishing a foundation of trust that is unattainable with general-purpose AI models.    
    \item \textbf{Foundation for Advanced AI:} Provides a structured, granular, and temporally-aware data model essential for AI systems to deterministically generate point-in-time compiled (unofficial consolidated) texts, compare provisions across versions, and understand the semantic evolution of legal concepts.
\end{itemize}

The proposed model—illustrated with examples from Brazilian legislation—establishes a robust foundation for next-generation legal information systems and addresses current limitations in AI’s handling of dynamic, component-level legal texts.

Future work will focus on four main areas:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Formal Ontological Development.} Create a comprehensive ontology that formally specifies all entities, subclasses, and relationships introduced in this model, aligning with existing standards such as LKIF-Core or LegalDocML.
    \item \textbf{Integration of Event-Centric Modeling.} Our model focuses on representing the versioned textual outcomes of legislative changes. A powerful future enhancement would be to explicitly model the \emph{legislative events} that trigger these version transitions. 
    Drawing inspiration from event-centric ontologies like the one proposed by Lima et al. 
    \cite{lima2008ontology} and the core \texttt{E5 Event} in CIDOC CRM, one could model an 
    "Amendment Event" as a distinct entity. This would allow for capturing richer contextual 
    information about the change itself, such as the cause and type of a change directly to its effect on the textual components.
    \item \textbf{Formal Comparative Analysis.} Conduct a formal analysis comparing the expressivity, computational tractability, and accuracy of inferring temporal states from implicit Akoma Ntoso metadata versus directly leveraging the explicit ontological entities proposed in this model. Such a study would provide strong empirical validation for the design choices presented in this paper.
    \item \textbf{Knowledge Graph Implementation and Tooling.} The proposed FRBRoo model is not 
    merely conceptual; it is designed to serve as the direct ontological schema for a large-scale, temporally-aware legal knowledge graph. The entities defined (Work, Expression, TV, CTV, etc.) and their relationships (\texttt{consolidates}, \texttt{derivesFromTemporalVersion}) map directly to the nodes and edges of such a graph. A primary direction for future work is therefore the practical implementation and population of this knowledge graph with historical legislation. This will involve developing automated parsing pipelines, component identification algorithms, and procedures for instantiating and linking the versioned entities, ultimately enabling a rigorous evaluation of the  model's utility for tasks like point-in-time text reconstruction and amendment impact tracing.
    \item \textbf{Advanced Reasoning Capabilities.} Build upon the structured knowledge graph \cite{colombo2024leveraging} to develop reasoning mechanisms—such as automated detection of normative conflicts or redundancies introduced by new amendments at the component level, and tracing the semantic drift of specific legal terms or concepts across components over time.
    \item \textbf{Rigorous Benchmarking for Deterministic Accuracy}. A critical future step is to develop evaluation benchmarks to rigorously test the model's primary success metric: its ability to perform flawless, deterministic point-in-time reconstruction of legal corpora. This will empirically validate the model's design philosophy, which consciously prioritizes verifiability and accuracy over other potential metrics, reflecting the non-negotiable demand for precision in the legal domain.
    \item \textbf{Integration with Natural Language Processing (NLP).} Explore integration with NLP techniques to enhance semantic understanding and processing of legal text changes.
\end{itemize}

By advancing these research directions, we aim to enable legal information systems that are more accurate, transparent, and capable of meeting the complex demands of legal practitioners, researchers, and AI-driven applications. 

\bigskip

Ultimately, the contribution of this paper extends beyond mere data organization. A robust descriptive 
model, such as the one proposed, provides the precise, versioned textual facts---the \emph{ground 
truth}---upon which higher-level legal reasoning rules (e.g., modeled in LKIF-Core) can operate. 
Without such an accurate and temporally-aware representation, any legal reasoning system would face ambiguity, outdated information, or a lack of verifiable input. Therefore, we frame this model as a \textbf{foundational prerequisite} for effective computational 
legal reasoning. It provides the essential factual layer for more advanced legal AI systems that 
perform automated analysis, compliance checking, and logical inference. This positioning elevates 
its importance, making it a critical component of a holistic legal AI architecture and opening clear 
pathways for collaborative research between the descriptive modeling and logical reasoning communities 
to drive interdisciplinary breakthroughs in the field.

title: BLITZSCALE: Fast and Live Large Model Autoscaling with O(1) Host Caching
summary:
Model autoscaling is the key mechanism to achieve serverless
model-as-a-service, but it faces a fundamental trade-off between scaling speed
and storage/memory usage to cache parameters, and cannot meet frequent scaling
requirements across multiple hosts. The key problem is that data plane
performance is slow, and scaled instances remain stopped while parameters are
loading. In this paper, we first show that the data plane can be made fast with
no or O(1) caching by loading parameters through the compute network between
GPUs because: (1) its speed is comparable to host cache and is underutilized,
and (2) scaling multiple instances requires no or O(1) caching with
network-optimized multicast. Second, autoscaling can be made live by breaking
the scaling abstraction for inference from a coarse-grained instance-level to a
fine-grained layer-level. This allows us to offload the layer computation from
the overloaded serving instances to the scaled ones without waiting for the
parameters to be fully loaded. Under real-world workloads, our system
BLITZSCALE achieves up to 94 % lower tail latency reductions compared to
state-of-the-art autoscaling system (ServerlessLLM), and it reduces the GPU
time used for serving by 49 % when compared with serving systems that do not
support autoscaling like DistServe and vLLM with the same
service-level-agreement.

bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the Eighteenth European Conference on Computer Systems
bib.abstract: As deep learning (DL) inference has been widely adopted for building user-facing applications in many domains, it is increasingly important for DL inference servers to achieve high throughput while preserving bounded latency. DL inference requests can be immediately served if the corresponding model is already in the GPU memory. Otherwise, it needs to load the model from host to GPU, adding a significant delay to inference. This paper proposes DeepPlan to minimize inference latency while provisioning DL models from host to GPU in server environments. First, we take advantage of the direct-host-access facility provided by commodity GPUs, allowing access to particular layers of models in the host memory directly from GPU without loading. Second, we parallelize model transmission across multiple GPUs to reduce the time for loading models from host to GPU. We show that a single inference can achieve a 1.94\texttimes{} speedup compared with the state-of-the-art pipelining approach for BERT-Base. When deploying multiple BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT-2 instances on a DL inference serving system, DeepPlan shows a significant performance improvement compared to the pipelining technique and stable 99\% tail latency.

title: Certifying Robustness via Topological Representations
summary:
We propose a neural network architecture that can learn discriminative
geometric representations of data from persistence diagrams, common descriptors
of Topological Data Analysis. The learned representations enjoy Lipschitz
stability with a controllable Lipschitz constant. In adversarial learning, this
stability can be used to certify $\epsilon$-robustness for samples in a
dataset, which we demonstrate on the ORBIT5K dataset representing the orbits of
a discrete dynamical system.

\section{Introduction}


In machine learning, the ability to obtain data representations that capture underlying geometrical and topological structures of data spaces is crucial. 
A common approach in Topological Data Analysis to extract multi-scale intrinsic geometric properties of data is persistent homology (PH) \citep{carlsson2009topology}. As a rich descriptor of  geometry,  PH has been used in machine learning pipelines in areas such as bioinformatics, neuroscience and material science \citep{dindin2020topological,colombo2022tool,lee_materialscience}. The key difference of PH compared to other methods in Geometric Deep Learning is perhaps the emphasis of theoretical stability results: PH is a Lipschitz function, with known Lipschitz constants, with respect to appropriate metrics on data and representation space \citep{cohen2005stability,skraba2020wasserstein}.

However, composing the PH pipeline with a neural network presents challenges with respect to the stability of the representations thus learned: they may lose stability or the stability may become insignificant in practice in case PH representations are composed with neural networks that have large Lipschitz constants. Moreover, the constant of the neural network may be difficult to compute or to control. While robustness to noise of PH-machine learning pipelines has been studied empirically \citep{turkevs2021noise}, we formulate the problem in the framework of adversarial learning and propose a neural network that can learn stable and discriminative geometric representations from persistence. Our contributions may be summarized as follows:

%with a controllable Lipschitz constant. In adversarial learning, the end-to-end stability can be used to certify $\epsilon$-robustness for samples in a dataset, which we demonstrate on the ORBIT5K data set representing the orbits of a discrete dynamical system.

\begin{itemize}
    \item We propose the Stable Rank Network (SRN), a neural network architecture taking PH as input, where the learned representations enjoy a Lipschitz property w.r.t.\ Wasserstein and Bottleneck metrics.
    \item

     We link the stability of the PH pipeline with robustness at test time for classifiers in adversarial learning. In particular we provide certified robustness for the SRN architecture.
    
   % We highlight a link to robustness at test time for classifiers in adversarial learning and show that the end-to-end stability of our PH pipeline can be used to certify $\epsilon$-robustness for samples in a dataset.
    \item On the ORBIT5K benchmark dataset, we demonstrate that the method can learn useful representations with certified robustness, when on the other hand integrating the PH pipeline with neural networks in a standard fashion can result in poor robustness properties.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Lipschitz neural networks and robustness at test time}
\label{subsec:LipNN}

The global Lipschitz constant of a deep neural network is typically very large and may be difficult to compute and control during training. Alternative networks may however be designed to enforce a Lipschitz property, while remaining trainable and expressive. In \cite{zhang2021towards}, the authors propose to replace the classical neuron in an MLP with a unit of the form:
\begin{equation*}
    u(x, w, b) = \|x - w\|_{\infty} + b,
\end{equation*}
where $w, b \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are trainable parameters and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the input. The unit is by design 1-Lipschitz w.r.t.\ the $L_\infty$ metric on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Such neurons are stacked to form a layer and layers are composed to form a neural network enjoying the same stability property.\\

%
Lipschitz neural networks will be used to prove robustness at test time, in the present context referring to the property of a method of maintaining the prediction under small metric perturbations of the input. We consider robustness of trained classifiers defined on a metric space. 
 Let $(\mathcal{X}, d_{\mathcal{X}})$ be a metric space and  $g: \mathcal{X} \to \{1, \ldots, C\}$ 
 a trained classifier on $\mathcal{X}$. 
 For a sample $x \in \mathcal{X}$ with ground truth label $c$, we say that $g$ is $\epsilon$-robust at $x$ if: 
 \[
    g(x') = c, \forall x' \in \mathcal{X} \text{ s.t. } d_{\mathcal{X}}(x,x') \leq \epsilon .
\]
We are interested in estimating the \emph{robustness radius} of $x$, that is the maximum $\epsilon$ for which $g$ is $\epsilon$-robust at $x$ sampled from the data distribution. The problem of computing the robustness radius for a data sample is NP-complete even for standard MLP classifiers \citep{katz2017reluplex}.

  \textit{Adversarial attacks} are methods designed to find small perturbations of a sample that lead to a wrong classification, thus yielding an upper bound for the robustness radius at the sample. %To counter adversarial attacks,

The field of \textit{certified robustness} \citep{li2023sok} provides instead lower bounds for the robustness radius at a data sample,  that is for a sample $x$ from the data distribution, an $\epsilon$ may be computed such that $g$ is $\epsilon$-robust at $x$.

The first step is a  vectorization using stable ranks (Section \ref{subsec:PH}), which depends on a learnable reparametrization of the filtration scale. The second step allows to learn interactions between points in the PD through a Lipschitz neural network (Section \ref{subsec:LipNN}).

The stable rank can be seen as a vectorization method for PDs which depends on parameters $(p,F)$, where $p\in[1,\infty]$ and $F: \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is an increasing bijection that can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the filtration scale used to apply persistent homology. For any choice of parameters $(p,F)$, with $F$ a $K$-Lipschitz function, the stable rank determines a function $r_{p,F}:\mathcal{PD} \to \mathbb{R}^\infty$ which enjoys the following Lipschitz condition:
\[
\| r_{p,F}(X) - r_{p,F}(Y)\|_\infty \le K \, W_p (X,Y),
\]
where $W_p$ denotes the $p$-Wasserstein distance between PDs  (see Appendix \ref{appendix:dists_pers_diags}).
If $F=\operatorname{id}$ is the identity on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, the corresponding Lipschitz constant is $K=1$, for any $p\in [1,\infty]$.

In practice, one chooses an appropriate subset $\mathcal{S}$ of $\mathcal{PD}$ and a sufficiently large integer $N$ such that $r_{p,F}$ can be viewed as a function $\mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}^N$. In our proposed SRN architecture, $F$ is parametrized with trainable weights and $r_{p,F}$ is followed by a Lipschitz neural network with inputs in $\mathbb{R}^N$ and outputs in $\mathbb{R}^C$. Since $r_{p,F}$ is $K$-Lipschitz and all layers of the Lipschitz neural network are $1$-Lipschitz functions, their composition $f$ is a $K$-Lipschitz function from $\mathcal{S}$ equipped with $W_p$ to $\mathbb{R}^C$ equipped with the $L_{\infty}$ metric.

If we now consider a classifier based on our neural network, $g = \operatorname{argmax} \circ f$, we can (following \cite{tsuzuku2018lipschitz}) conclude that $g$ is $\epsilon$-robust at $x$ for all $\epsilon \geq \frac{M_x}{2K}$, where $K$ is the Lipschitz constant of $f$ and $M_x$ is the prediction margin of $f$ at $x$, defined as the difference between the largest logit (corresponding to the correct class) and the second largest logit: $     M_x = f(x)_c - \max_{i \neq c} f(x)_i$. Thus since the Lipschitz constant $K$ is known, computing a lower bound for the robustness radius at a sample $x$ only requires a forward pass of $x$ in the neural network to get $M_x$.

If the Lipschitz constant of $g$ is not known, we estimate robustness of the classifier by searching for adversarial examples. \section{Results }
\label{sec:results}

We train SRN (see Appendix \ref{appendix:impl_details_sr_linf} for details) on the ORBIT5K dataset, using only PDs corresponding to degree-$1$ homology $H_1$, and we choose stability w.r.t.\ $W_\infty$ by setting $p=\infty$. In Table \ref{tab:accs_all_methods} the accuracy of the method is compared to various accuracies reported for other methods on the same problem, showing that despite the constraint of learning a Lipschitz function, competitive performance may be achieved.




We then reimplement Perslay using only $H_1$ PDs as input (achieving accuracy of $84.4 \pm 0.6$). In Table \ref{tab:rob_accs}, we report for various values of $\epsilon$, the percentage of samples in the test set such that the method described in Section \ref{advmethod} fails to produce an adversarial example within a radius of $\epsilon$ w.r.t.\ $W_\infty$. This constitutes an upper bound of the robust accuracy. While the method achieves high accuracy for the test samples, it degrades significantly even for very small $\epsilon$-neighborhoods around the samples. To get an idea of the scale we show the average intra-class and inter-class distances in Table \ref{tab:avgdisth1}. While adversarial examples are common for various types of data and neural networks, the geometry of Wasserstein metrics (e.g.\ the presence, arbitrarily close to any PD, of PDs where points are added close to the diagonal) may result in particularly poor robustness at test time.


%While in Section \ref{sec:rob_test_limits} we had to upper-bound the $\epsilon$-robustness by finding adversarial examples at distance $\epsilon$, we can now find a meaningful lower bound, meaning we can certify that no adversarial example exists within that distance.

In the case of SRN, for a sample in the test set, instead of trying to find adversarial examples, we can directly compute its certified $\epsilon$-robustness following Section \ref{SRN}. For various threshold values of $\epsilon$ we can then compute a lower bound of the robust accuracy by computing the percentage of samples in the test set for which the $\epsilon$-robustness is above this threshold (Table \ref{tab:rob_accs}). Because of this, the robust accuracies of SRN are underestimates whereas for Perslay they are overestimates. Despite this, the robust accuracies are higher for SRN and the $\epsilon$-radii appear to be meaningful compared to the average distances in Table \ref{tab:avgdisth1}.

\subsection{Persistence diagrams}
\label{subsec:PDs}

Consider the subset $U := \{(a,b)\in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\times [0,\infty ] \mid a\leq b\}$ of the extended plane. 
A \emph{persistence diagram} $D$ is a multiset of elements of $U$, which in this work we assume to be finite. By definition of multiset, $D$ is a pair $(X,\mu)$, where $X$ is a finite subset of $U$ and $\mu : X \to \mathbb{N}_{>0}$ is a function, interpreted as a multiplicity function. The cardinality of $D$, denoted by $\operatorname{rank}(D)$, is $\sum_{x\in X}\mu (x)$. A persistence diagram $D$ can be viewed as the set $\{ (x,i_x)\in X\times \mathbb{N}_{>0} \mid 1\le i_x \le \mu (x) \}$. In what follows, for simplicity we disregard the second components of the elements $(x,i_x)$ of $D$, using the notation $D=\{x_i\}_{i = 1, \ldots ,\operatorname{rank}(D)}$, with $x_i=(a_i,b_i)\in U$, where it may happen that $x_j=x_k$ for some $j\ne k$. We use the notation $\mathcal{PD}$ for the collection of all persistence diagrams.

%\textcolor{red}{(How are PDs obtained: brief sketch of TDA pipeline, to introduce $H_q$ and alpha complexes. This part can be improved)}

In topological data analysis \citep{carlsson2009topology}, persistence diagrams are usually obtained by applying $q$-th simplicial homology $H_q$ (for some $q\in \mathbb{N}$) to a nested sequence $K_0\subseteq K_1 \subseteq \cdots$ of simplicial complexes, called a filtration, associated with the data. Details on the pipeline of persistent homology and on various constructions to transform the data into a filtration of simplicial complexes are included for example in \cite{otter2017roadmap,oudot2017persistence}. In this work, the data is in the form of point clouds, which are transformed into filtrations of simplicial complexes using the alpha-complex construction \citep{edelsbrunner1995union}.  

%\textcolor{red}{(Finiteness hypothesis for this work: PDs have only finite bars. We only use this for stable rank (e.g. not for PersLay? or yes?), so maybe move to stable rank section?)}

An element $x=(a,b)$ of a persistence diagram is called a \emph{point at infinity} if $b=\infty$. In this work, all persistence diagrams we consider do not have points at infinity. Starting from point cloud data and using the Alpha complex construction and simplicial homology $H_q$, one always obtains persistence diagrams without points at infinity for every $q>0$.

\subsection{Wasserstein distance between persistence diagrams} 
\label{appendix:dists_pers_diags}

Let $U$ be the subset of the extended plane defined in Section \ref{subsec:PDs}, and consider its subset $\Delta :=  \{ (a,a) \mid a \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \}$.  For all $p\in [1,\infty]$, let $d_p (x,y) :=  \left\| x-y \right\|_p$ for all $x,y\in U$, and let $d_p (x,\Delta) :=  \inf_{z\in \Delta} d_p (x,z)$, for all $x\in U$. 
%As is easy to show, if $x=(a,b)$, then $d_p (x,\Delta)= d_p (x,\overline{z})$ with $\overline{z}\coloneqq  (\frac{a+b}{2},\frac{a+b}{2})$.

For $p\in [1,\infty]$, the $p$-\emph{Wasserstein distance} between two persistence diagrams $D=\{x_i\}_{i=1,\ldots, m}$ and $D'=\{x'_j\}_{j=1,\ldots, n}$ is defined by
\begin{multline*}
W_p (D,D') :=  \\
\inf_{\alpha} \left\| \left( \left\| (d_p (x_i,x'_{\alpha (i)}))_{i\in I} \right\|_p , \left\| (d_p (x_i,\Delta))_{i\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\setminus I} \right\|_p , \left\| (d_p (\Delta, x'_j))_{j\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}\setminus \alpha (I)} \right\|_p  \right) \right\|_p ,
\end{multline*}
where the infimum is over all injective functions $\alpha \colon  I \to \{1,\ldots ,n\}$, with $I\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,m\}$.

The \emph{Bottleneck distance}, which is of special importance in the literature on persistent homology, is the distance $W_{\infty}$ corresponding to the case $p=\infty$. We remark that the definition of $p$-Wasserstein distance we use here differs from that of some other authors, which use the metric $d_{\infty}$ on $U$, for all $p\in [1,\infty]$ (see e.g.\ \cite{cohen2010lipschitz}).

Persistence diagrams enjoy crucial stability properties. 
For example, consider a filtration of simplicial complexes constructed as a sublevel-set filtration of a simplicial complex equipped with a function on its set of simplices. Under mild assumptions on this function, the Bottleneck distance on persistence diagrams is stable w.r.t.\ perturbations of the function in $L_{\infty}$ norm \citep{cohen2005stability}. Stability results also exist for other types of data from which a filtration of simplicial complexes may be constructed, e.g.\ Gromov-Hausdorff distance between point clouds. An account of stability results involving the $p$-Wasserstein distance is given in \citep{skraba2020wasserstein}.

\section{Stable ranks}

\paragraph{Definition of stable ranks}
In this section, all persistence diagrams are assumed to have no points at infinity.
Let $V := \{(a,b)\in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^2 \mid a\leq b\}$ be the subset of $U$ (see Section \ref{subsec:PDs}) obtained by removing all points at infinity. Let $F:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be an increasing bijection, which we call a \emph{reparameterization} of $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. Parametrized families of increasing bijections can be produced from regular contours introduced in \cite{chacholski2020metrics}. 
Given a persistence diagram $D\in \mathcal{PD}$, let $F(D)$ denote the persistence diagram obtained by transforming each point $x=(a,b)$ of $D$ into the point $F(x):=(F(a),F(b))$.
The \emph{stable rank} of a persistence diagram $D$ with parameters $(p,F)$, where $p\in [1,\infty]$ and $F$ is a reparameterization of $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, is the function $\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D): \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{N}$ defined by
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D)(t) := \min \{\operatorname{rank}(D') \mid D'\in \mathcal{PD} \text{ and } W_p(F(D),F(D'))\le t \},
\]
where $W_p$ denotes the $p$-Wasserstein distance between persistence diagrams and $\operatorname{rank}(D')$ denotes the cardinality of the persistence diagram $D'$ (or, equivalently, of $F(D')$). The function $\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D)$ is nonincreasing and piecewise constant. One way to compare such functions is via the \emph{interleaving distance} $d_{\bowtie}$, see \cite[Def.~9.1]{scolamiero2017multidimensional}. Stable ranks were originally defined for persistence modules (see \cite{scolamiero2017multidimensional, chacholski2020metrics}), algebraic objects which are completely described (up to isomorphism) by the associated persistence diagrams. The stable ranks we introduce here for persistence diagrams can be regarded as an instance of the original definition thanks to the equivalence of Wasserstein distances between persistence modules and persistence diagrams detailed in \cite[Sect.~4.4]{agerberg2023algebraic}. 

\paragraph{Computation of stable ranks}
Let $\ell_F : V \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ denote the function defined by $\ell_F(a,b):= F(b)-F(a)$, which we call the \emph{lifetime function} induced by the reparameterization $F$.
Let $D=\{x_i\}_{i=1,\ldots, m}$ be a persistence diagram such that $x_i =(a_i,b_i)\in V$, for all $i\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}$, and suppose that its points are ordered non-decreasingly by their lifetime $\ell_F$, meaning that $\ell_F (a_1,b_1)\le \ell_F(a_2,b_2)\le \cdots \le \ell_F(a_m,b_m)$. 
Then, by \cite[Prop.~5.1]{agerberg2023algebraic}, for any fixed $p\in [1,\infty)$ there exist real numbers $0=t_0 < t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_m$ such that the function $\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D) \colon  \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{N}$ is constant on the intervals $[t_0,t_1)$, $[t_1,t_2)$,\ldots , $[t_{m-1},t_m)$, $[t_m,\infty)$, with values
$\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D)(t_j) = \operatorname{rank} (D) - j$,
for every $j\in \{0,1,\ldots ,m\}$. Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:tj}
t_j= 2^{\frac{1-p}{p}}\left\| ( \ell_F(a_1,b_1),\ldots ,\ell_F(a_j,b_j) )\right\|_p 
\end{equation}
for every $j\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}$.

For $p=\infty$, the sequence of real numbers $(t_j)_j$ defined in Equation (\ref{eq:tj}) (setting $2^{\frac{1-p}{p}}=2^{-1}$) only satisfies $0=t_0 \le t_1 \le t_2 \le \cdots \le t_m$ instead of strict inequalities. Letting $s_k$ denote the $k^{\text{th}}$ smallest value in $\{ t_j\}_j$ one obtains a sequence $0=s_0 < s_1 < s_2 < \cdots < s_{m'}$ such that the stable rank with parameters $(p=\infty,F)$ is constant on the intervals $[s_0,s_1)$,\ldots , $[s_{m'},\infty)$, with values 
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{\infty, F}(D)(s_k) = \operatorname{rank} (D) - \max \{j \mid t_j=s_k \} .
\]

For any fixed $p\in [1,\infty]$, the function $\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D)$ can be represented as a vector $r_{p,F}(D) = (r_0, r_1, \ldots ,r_m) \in \mathbb{R}^{m+1}$, where
\[
r_i := t_{m-i} = 2^{\frac{1-p}{p}} \| (\ell_F(a_1,b_1) , \ldots ,\ell_F(a_{m-i},b_{m-i})) \|_p, 
\]
for all $i\in \{0,\ldots ,m-1\}$, and $r_m := 0$. We remark that, thanks to the assumption that the persistence diagram $D$ has no points at infinity, all $t_j$ and all $r_i$ are real numbers. By construction (see \cite[Sect.~5]{agerberg2023algebraic}), the entries of $r_{p,F}(D)$ satisfy $r_i = \min \{t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \mid \widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D) \le i\}$, for all $i\in \{0,\ldots ,m\}$. 

\paragraph{Computing distances between stable ranks}
Since $m=\operatorname{rank}(D)$ depends on the persistence diagram $D$, to compare the vectors $r_{p,F}(D)\in \mathbb{R}^{m+1}$ associated with different persistence diagrams we regard them as elements of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^\infty$ of finite sequences over $\mathbb{R}$, defined by
\[
\mathbb{R}^\infty := \{ (r_0,r_1, \ldots) \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}\mid \text{finitely many entries $r_i$ are nonzero}\}, 
\]
with the natural vector space structure given by entry-wise addition and scalar multiplication. Any vector $r_{p,F}(D)=(r_0,r_1,\ldots ,r_m)\in \mathbb{R}^{m+1}$ is regarded as the element $(r_0,r_1,\ldots ,r_m, 0, \ldots)$ of $\mathbb{R}^{\infty}$, which we will also denote by $r_{p,F}$ with a small abuse of notation. 

Importantly, as a consequence of the results in \cite[Sect.~5]{agerberg2023algebraic}, the interleaving distance between stable ranks can be computed via the $L_{\infty}$ metric in $\mathbb{R}^{\infty}$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:interleavingLinfty}
d_{\bowtie}(\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D),\widehat{\operatorname{rank}}_{p,F}(D')) = \| r_{p,F}(D) - r_{p,F}(D')\|_{\infty},
\end{equation}
for any $D,D'\in \mathcal{PD}$. 


In practice, when using stable ranks in data analysis we work on a subset $\mathcal{S}\subset \mathcal{PD}$ of persistence diagrams which allows us to compare the vectors $\{r_{p,F}(D)\}_{D\in \mathcal{S}}$ via Equation (\ref{eq:interleavingLinfty}) in a finite dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (for a sufficiently large $d$) instead of $\mathbb{R}^{\infty}$. For example, in many practical situations one can consider $\mathcal{S}=\{D\in \mathcal{PD} \mid \operatorname{rank}(D) \le d-1\}$, for a fixed and sufficiently large $d$.
